newsitem.title: USA: Russia has big G7 role, economic challenges remain.
newsitem.headline: Russia has big G7 role, economic challenges remain.

text.p: Russian officials left the begging bowl at home during the Denver Group of Seven summit this weekend, confirming Russia's growing maturity in world leaders' political and economic talks.
But official forecasts of economic growth next year and a promise to let Russia join the creditor nations' Paris Club cannot quite hide the challenges ahead.

The G7 nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- are not ready to let Russia take part in talks about financial and macro-economic issues during their annual summits and they want Russia to do more to reform its cumbersome tax system and clarify rules for foreign investors.

"There is a consensus among the Group of Seven rich nations that they need to continue meeting without Russia to discuss economic and financial issues," said Catherine Colonna, spokeswoman to French President Jacques Chirac.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told a news conference that the Russian economic picture was encouraging, but he noted that Russia was still borrowing money from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.

"There are financial and economic issues in which the Western industrialised countries are in a different position to what Russia is now," Rubin said. "It is more fruitful to have discussions amongst those who share that commonality, and that's why the finance ministers met as a G7."

The meeting, called the "Summit of the Eight" to reflect Russia's rising role, nevertheless gave President Boris Yeltsin a full say in political discussions and allowed reform chief Anatoly Chubais to highlight Russia's economic gains.

The Kremlin's confident showing was in stark contrast to Yeltsin's first appearances at the rich nations' club in 1992 and 1993, when he won promises for billions of dollars in loans and aid to help revive a faltering economy.

This time officials announced that Russia -- a big debtor in its own right -- had won agreement in principle to join the Paris Club, raising hopes that Moscow could recoup some of the billions of dollars lent to its developing country allies in Soviet days.
Chubais said this could boost Russia's credit rating, allowing it to borrow money more cheaply on international debt markets.
"We would be given a higher rating now than we were at the end of last year," he said. "We will apply again next fall and I believe Russia's rating will rise."

Russia has a Ba2 rating from Moody's, BB- from S&P and BB+ from IBCA. It raised $2 billion last week with a 10-year Eurobond, its thid issue as a sovereign borrower and the largest single issue from an emerging market economy.
Chubais said Russia could have doubled the volume of its Eurobond without any problems. "They probably would have offered us $4 billion, but at the moment we do not need that," he said.
Russia also wants membership of the World Trade Organisation and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, and Yeltsin said he believed WTO membership could come this year.
U.S. officials say Moscow has not yet taken all steps needed for membership and Rubin has targeted 1998 for Russia to join the WTO.
Chubais, one of two reformist first deputy prime ministers, said the Russian economy would return to growth next year.
"For the first time we are on the real eve of economic growth, which means the growth of standards of living...and I am sure that 1998 will be the first year of Russian economic growth," he said.
Output has halved in the years since Russia launched its economic reform programme, designed to turn the communist-era centrally planned economy into a market system.
There have been countless forecasts that the economy is poised to grow, but investment remains stubbornly low and millions of workers survive for months without pay.
Chubais conceded that one-fifth of Russians were living below the poverty line but he said Russia had already become a "viable and capitalist society".
Asked if communism was dead in Russia, he replied: "Absolutely."
